around.headline: Twist in Bengaluru kidnapping case: in-laws allegedly plotted woman's abduction
around.summary: Police say a Rajasthan family plotted the abduction of a woman from Bengaluru after she married a man of her choice, tracking her husband before the car chase, per The Times of India and NDTV. If a family member is being coerced or confined over a personal choice like marriage, report it to police (100) rather than treating it as a private family matter.

around.summary: Authorities booked thousands of cases against private bus operators after complaints of passengers being charged well above the printed fare, per The Times of India. Always insist on a ticket — it's your only proof if you need to complain to the transport department later.

around.summary: The department booked over 1,500 cases for violations during festival-period checks across the state, per The Hindu. Keep your RC, licence, insurance and helmet in order if you're driving through checkpoints this week.

around.summary: A dispute over royalty rates has forced quarries, stone crushers and M-Sand units to down shutters statewide, per The Times of India. If you're mid-construction or renovation, expect sand and aggregate supply delays and possible price bumps until it's resolved.

around.summary: Multiplex operators are pushing back against a state proposal to add a 2% cess on movie tickets, per The Times of India. If it goes through, expect a small bump on your next multiplex outing.

street_smart.title: You board a private bus out of Bengaluru for a weekend trip during the festive rush. The conductor doesn't hand out a ticket and asks for nearly double the printed fare, saying 'everyone's paying this because of the rush.' What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Today's real news: Karnataka authorities booked 3,756 cases against private buses over steep fare overcharging complaints (The Times of India). Transport-fare overcharging hasn't been used as a street-smart topic in the last three weeks.
street_smart.situation: The bus is about to leave, other passengers seem to be paying up without protest, and arguing risks being left behind at the stand.

choices.text: Pay the higher amount in cash and skip asking for a ticket — arguing would waste time and you still need to reach your destination.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Without a ticket you have no proof of what you actually paid, so there's nothing to attach to a complaint — and it quietly normalizes the overcharge for the next passenger too.

choices.text: Insist on a ticket at the printed fare before paying; if the conductor won't budge, pay to avoid being stranded but note the bus registration number and operator name to file a complaint afterward.
choices.feedback: Correct. A ticket (or at least a photo of the fare chart and bus number) is what turns 'I was overcharged' into a complaint the transport department can actually act on, without you missing your ride.

choices.text: Refuse to pay and get off the bus at the stand to find another one.
choices.feedback: Risky if you're on a tight schedule or it's late — you may end up stranded with fewer options, and it does nothing to stop the same overcharging for other passengers who do board.

choices.text: Argue loudly with the conductor in front of other passengers to shame them into charging the correct fare.
choices.feedback: Risky. A public confrontation with no documentation can escalate quickly and rarely gets you a refund — you're better off paying, documenting, and complaining through the proper channel.

takeaways: Always ask for a ticket — it's your main evidence if you need to report overcharging later.
Karnataka's transport department and RTO helplines take complaints against bus operators if you have the bus registration number and route details.
Photograph the fare chart displayed inside the bus and the registration plate before you board if a ticket isn't offered upfront.
